chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Hammad ibn Uthman, from Abd al-Rahim al-Qasir, who said:

I wrote, along with Abd al-Malik ibn Ayn, to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), asking him about faith (Iman), what it is. So he wrote to me, along with Abd al-Malik ibn Ayn: 'You asked, may Allah have mercy on you, about faith; and faith is affirmation by the tongue, and a firm conviction in the heart, and action by the limbs. And faith is one part from another, and it is a house (domain), and similarly Islam is a house, and disbelief is a house.'

So the servant may be a Muslim before he is a believer, and he does not become a believer until he becomes a Muslim. So Islam precedes faith, and it shares with faith. So when the servant commits a major sin from the major sins, or a minor sin from the minor sins which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, forbade, he exits from faith; the name of faith drops from him, while the name of Islam remains established upon him.

So if he repents and seeks forgiveness, he returns to the house of faith. And nothing drives him out to disbelief except denial (Juhud) and legalization (Istihlal) — that he says of the permissible, 'This is forbidden,' and of the forbidden, 'This is permissible,' and accepts that as religion. At that point, he exits from Islam and faith, entering into disbelief. And he is like the one who enters the Sanctuary (Haram), then enters the Ka'bah, and defecates in the Ka'bah; so he is expelled from the Ka'bah and from the Sanctuary, his neck is struck, and he goes to the Fire.

key_terms.الْإِسْتِحْلَالُ: Legalization (considering something permissible that is forbidden)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between Islam and Iman in Shia theology, and how do sins affect a believer's status?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi articulates the Shia doctrine of 'gradual exit' (takhallu), distinguishing between the external submission of Islam and the internal, comprehensive state of Iman, which includes both belief and righteous action. It establishes that major or minor sins remove one from the 'house of faith' while retaining the title of Muslim, whereas denial (jukhud) or legalization of the forbidden (istihlal) results in total expulsion into disbelief, a concept central to the Maturidi and Shia theological debates on the status of the sinner.
